theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Before you start a dessert from the standard recipe, what should you do first?
options: Read the whole recipe and set out what you need
Start mixing and read each step as you reach it
Change the amounts to suit your own taste
Switch on the mixer so the motor warms up

questions.stem: Why are the ingredients for cakes and pastry weighed on a scale, not measured by eye?
options: Scales make the food taste sweeter
It is quicker than reading the recipe
Baking needs exact amounts to work
Weighed flour never needs to be sifted

questions.stem: Why should the oven be preheated before you mix a cake batter?
options: So the kitchen warms up and the butter melts
So it is at the right heat when the batter is ready
So the cake can bake with the door left open
So the oven light can be checked first

questions.stem: What does sifting flour or icing sugar do?
options: Makes them sweeter and darker
Kills all the germs in them
Turns them into a smooth paste
Removes lumps and adds air

questions.stem: In the creaming method for a cake, which two ingredients are beaten together first until light and fluffy?

Milk and baking powder

options: To stop the mix curdling (splitting)
To make the cake turn a darker colour
So that fewer eggs are needed overall
To cool the mixture down for the oven

questions.stem: What does "folding in" mean, for example when adding flour to a whisked sponge mix?
options: Beating hard with an electric mixer for five minutes
Stirring quickly round and round with a fork
Kneading the mixture on a floured board
Gently cutting and turning the mix to keep the air in

options: Grease makes the whites turn yellow
Grease stops the whites from foaming up
Grease makes the meringue taste much too sweet
Grease makes the whites set too hard

questions.stem: When making meringue, when should the sugar be added to the egg whites?
options: All at once, before you start whisking the whites
Gradually, once the whites are foamy
After the meringue has been baked
Only if the whites will not foam up

questions.stem: Cream for piping has been whipped for too long. What happens to it?

It turns pink and starts to smell sour

questions.stem: Which cream whips best for piping and filling desserts?

Warm single cream left out on the counter

questions.stem: How should leaf gelatine be prepared before it is added to a mousse?

Add it dry, straight from the packet
Freeze it, then grate it into the mix
Soak it in cold water, squeeze it, then melt it gently

questions.stem: A jelly made with fresh pineapple will not set. Why?

Pineapple is too cold when it is first cut
The pineapple juice is too thick to set
An enzyme in fresh pineapple breaks down gelatine

questions.stem: A guest is vegetarian. Which setting agent, made from seaweed, can be used instead of gelatine?

Agar
Suet

It turns a dark brown colour

questions.stem: Why is a crème caramel baked in a bain-marie (a tray of hot water) in the oven?

The water adds extra liquid to the custard
The water cools the oven so it uses less gas
The water makes the caramel go hard and crisp

questions.stem: What is the safest way to melt chocolate for a dessert?

In boiling water, stirred in with a whisk
In a hot oven, left uncovered for an hour
In a bowl over a pan of simmering water

options: It was stirred with a clean, dry spatula
It was melted too slowly and gently
A drop of water or steam got into it
It was kept warm, but not too hot

questions.stem: Why must you take great care when making caramel?

Hot sugar sticks to the skin and burns badly

It makes the pastry taste sweeter

It firms the fat and stops shrinking

questions.stem: Why should cream desserts on a buffet be set out in small amounts and topped up often?

questions.stem: A tray of mousse is made the day before a villa dinner. How should it be stored?

questions.stem: A guest asks if the pudding contains gluten, and you are not sure. What should you do?

Tell the guest to pick out any gluten

questions.stem: Which plate should be used for a cold dessert such as ice cream or mousse?
options: A plate warmed in the oven
A chilled plate
A plate from the hot cupboard
A plate still wet from washing

questions.stem: When should icing sugar be dusted over a moist dessert such as a fruit tart?

Before baking, so that it browns

questions.stem: Which garnish is most suitable for a plated mango mousse?

questions.stem: Why should a cake be cut using a portion marker or guide?

So the cake stays warm for longer

questions.stem: You need to scrape down the bowl of a stand mixer. What must you do first?

options: Wipe it over with a dry cloth only
Spray sanitiser straight over the food scraps and leave it
Scrape, wash with detergent, rinse, sanitise and dry

essays.stem: Describe how you would plan and prepare (mise en place) for a plated dessert course for a villa dinner of 12 guests.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would check the menu, the number of guests and any allergies or special diets, and read the standard recipe for each part of the dessert. I would scale the recipe for 12 portions, plus one or two spare, and write a list of the ingredients and equipment I need. I would check that the ingredients are in stock, in date and of good quality, and take out only what I need. Then I would plan a time order. For example, a mousse must be made hours ahead so that it can set, a sauce can be made earlier and chilled, and fruit is cut close to service. I would weigh and measure every ingredient before I start, preheat the oven, and prepare the tins, moulds, piping bags and garnishes. For a cold dessert I would chill the plates. Last, I would keep my station clean and organised, and tell the chef at once if anything is missing.
markingPoints: Checks the menu, numbers and allergies, and reads the standard recipe
Scales the recipe and lists the ingredients and equipment
Checks stock, dates and quality
Plans a time order (setting and chilling times, fruit cut close to service)
Weighs and measures everything, preheats the oven, and prepares equipment, plates and garnishes

essays.stem: Explain how to whip cream for piping, and how to whisk egg whites for a meringue. Say what can go wrong with each.
essays.modelAnswer: To whip cream, I use chilled whipping cream or heavy cream in a cold, clean bowl. I whisk steadily until it thickens and holds its shape. For folding into a mousse I stop at soft peaks, and for piping I stop when it just holds a firm peak. If I whip it for too long, the cream turns grainy and starts to turn into butter, and it can no longer be piped smoothly. For meringue, the bowl and whisk must be very clean and free of grease, and there must be no egg yolk in the whites, because fat stops them foaming. I whisk the whites until they are foamy, then add the sugar a little at a time while I keep whisking, until the meringue is thick, glossy and holds stiff peaks. If the sugar goes in too early or all at once, the meringue may not reach its full volume, and if the sugar does not dissolve, the meringue can weep sugary drops after baking.
markingPoints: Cream: chilled cream with enough fat, in a cold, clean bowl
Stops at soft peaks for folding and firm peaks for piping; over-whipped cream turns grainy or to butter
Egg whites: clean, grease-free bowl and no yolk
Whisks to foamy, then adds sugar gradually to stiff, glossy peaks
Says what goes wrong if the sugar is added too early, all at once, or does not dissolve

essays.stem: Describe how to make a set dessert, such as a mango mousse, using gelatine. Include how to use the gelatine correctly.
essays.modelAnswer: First I weigh all the ingredients and prepare the moulds or glasses. I soak leaf gelatine in cold water for a few minutes until it is soft, then squeeze out the water. If I use powdered gelatine, I sprinkle it over a little cold water and leave it to swell. I purée the mango and sweeten it. I melt the soaked gelatine gently in a little warm purée, stirring until it has dissolved, but I do not let it boil, because boiling weakens its setting power. I stir the gelatine into the rest of the mango purée. Then I whip the cream to soft peaks and fold it gently into the purée to keep the air in. If the recipe uses uncooked egg whites, they should be pasteurised. I pour the mix into the moulds, then cover, label and chill them at 5 °C or below until set, usually several hours. I would not add fresh pineapple or papaya, because their enzymes stop gelatine from setting.
markingPoints: Soaks leaf gelatine in cold water and squeezes it (or swells powdered gelatine in cold water)
Dissolves the gelatine gently without boiling
Folds the whipped cream in gently to keep the air in
Covers, labels and chills at 5 °C or below until set
Notes that fresh pineapple or papaya stop gelatine setting, or that uncooked egg should be pasteurised

essays.stem: Explain how to make a crème anglaise (custard sauce), how to tell when it is cooked, and how to stop it from curdling.
essays.modelAnswer: Crème anglaise is a pouring custard made from milk (or milk and cream), egg yolks, sugar and vanilla. First I heat the milk with the vanilla until it is just below boiling. In a bowl I whisk the egg yolks and sugar together until pale. I pour a little of the hot milk onto the yolks while whisking, to warm them slowly, then add the rest. I pour the mix back into a clean pan and cook it over a low heat, stirring all the time with a wooden spoon or spatula, especially round the bottom and edges. It is cooked when it thickens enough to coat the back of the spoon, and a line drawn through it with a finger stays clear. It must never boil, or the egg will scramble and the sauce will curdle. To stop this, I keep the heat low, stir all the time, and strain it into a cold bowl as soon as it is cooked. If it is not served at once, I cool it quickly, cover it and chill it.
markingPoints: Correct ingredients: milk or cream, egg yolks, sugar and vanilla
Warms the milk and adds it to the yolks slowly while whisking
Cooks gently over a low heat, stirring all the time
Cooked when it coats the back of a spoon; it must not boil
Strains into a cold bowl, and cools quickly and chills if not served at once

essays.stem: Describe two traditional Jamaican desserts: their main ingredients and how each is made. Then explain how you would present one of them for hotel guests.
essays.modelAnswer: Sweet potato pudding is made from grated sweet potato mixed with coconut milk, brown sugar, a little flour, and spices such as nutmeg, cinnamon and vanilla, sometimes with raisins. The mix is poured into a greased tin and baked until it is firm, with a soft, custard-like layer on top. It is cooled before it is cut. Gizzada is a small tart. A short pastry case is pinched round the edge to make a crimped crust, then filled with grated coconut cooked with brown sugar, nutmeg and ginger, and baked until the pastry is golden. To present sweet potato pudding for hotel guests, I would cut neat, equal squares with a portion guide and place one slightly off-centre on a clean plate. I would add a quenelle of whipped cream or coconut ice cream, a little caramel sauce and a few slices of fresh fruit. I would wipe the rim, and tell the guests what the dessert is and which allergens it contains.
markingPoints: First dessert with its correct main ingredients
Correct method for the first dessert
Second dessert with its correct main ingredients and method
Presentation: a neat, equal portion with a suitable accompaniment, sauce and garnish
Clean plate rim, and allergen information for the guests

essays.stem: Explain the main points of good dessert presentation on a plate.
essays.modelAnswer: A plated dessert should look attractive, taste good and be easy to eat. First, the plate must be clean, the right size and the right temperature: chilled for cold desserts like mousse or ice cream, and warm for hot desserts like bread pudding. The portion should follow the standard recipe, so that every guest gets the same. The main item is the focus of the plate, often placed slightly off-centre, with the sauce, garnish and any accompaniment arranged around it. Good presentation uses contrast of colour (white cream with bright mango coulis), texture (soft mousse with a crisp tuile) and height. Everything on the plate must be edible and should match the flavour of the dessert, such as fresh fruit or a mint leaf. The plate should not be overloaded: some empty space looks neat. Icing sugar is dusted just before service, and the rim is wiped clean. Hot and cold parts, such as warm pudding with ice cream, are put together at the last moment so that the dessert reaches the guest at its best.
markingPoints: A clean plate of the right size and temperature
The portion follows the standard recipe
A clear focus, with balance and some space on the plate
Contrast of colour, texture and height, with edible garnishes that match the flavour
Finishing at the last moment: dusting, wiping the rim, and putting hot and cold parts together

essays.stem: Explain how to store desserts safely, including cream desserts, desserts made with uncooked eggs, frozen desserts and leftovers.
essays.modelAnswer: Desserts with cream, custard, mousse or fresh fruit are high-risk foods, because germs grow quickly in them when they are warm. They must be covered, labelled with the name and date, and kept in the fridge at 5 °C or below, or as the Centre's food safety plan says. They are stored above or apart from raw foods such as meat and eggs, so that nothing drips onto them. Hot desserts and baked custards that will be served cold are cooled quickly and then chilled. Uncooked desserts that use eggs, such as some mousses, should be made with pasteurised eggs. Ice cream and sorbet are kept in the freezer at about −18 °C or colder. Ice cream that has melted must not be refrozen; it is thrown away. On a buffet, cream desserts are set out in small amounts and topped up from the fridge. Stock is used in date order, first in, first out, and leftovers that have stood out at room temperature are thrown away, not kept.
markingPoints: Cream, custard and fruit desserts are high risk: covered, labelled and chilled at 5 °C or below
Kept apart from raw foods; hot desserts cooled quickly before chilling
Pasteurised eggs for uncooked desserts
Frozen at about −18 °C or colder; melted ice cream is never refrozen
Small amounts on buffets, first in first out, and leftovers from room temperature thrown away

essays.stem: A villa guest has a severe nut allergy, and another guest eats no gluten. Describe how you would prepare and serve their desserts safely.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would get the details from the guests or the booking, and tell the chef. I would check the standard recipe and the label of every ingredient, including chocolate, biscuits, garnishes and sauces, for nuts and for gluten (from wheat, barley and rye), and for warnings such as "may contain nuts". If an ingredient is not safe, I would choose a different dessert or a safe swap, such as a fruit dessert, or one made with gluten-free flour. I would wash my hands and make the allergy-free desserts first, on a cleaned and sanitised surface, with clean bowls, tools and piping bags. I would keep them covered and away from the other desserts, and label them with the guest's name. At service, they go straight to the right guest, and the server tells the guest what they are. If I am ever unsure whether something is safe, I ask the chef rather than guess, because an allergic reaction can be very serious.
markingPoints: Gets the details and tells the chef
Checks recipes and labels, including garnishes and "may contain" warnings
Chooses a safe dessert or safe swaps
Prevents cross-contact: makes them first with clean equipment and surfaces, kept apart and labelled
Serves them to the right guest, and asks rather than guesses if unsure

essays.stem: Describe how to make and bake a sweet short pastry case for a fruit tart, including blind baking.
essays.modelAnswer: I weigh the flour, butter, sugar and egg exactly. I sift the flour, then rub the cold butter into it with my fingertips until it looks like fine breadcrumbs, and stir in the sugar. I bind it with beaten egg, and a little cold water if needed, and press it together without kneading, because overworking makes the pastry tough. I wrap it and rest it in the fridge for about 30 minutes, or as the recipe says, so that the fat firms and the pastry does not shrink. Then I roll it out evenly on a lightly floured surface, line a greased tin, press it into the edges and trim the top. I prick the base with a fork and rest it again. To blind bake, I line the pastry with baking paper, fill it with baking beans, and bake it in a preheated oven as the recipe says until the edges are set. I remove the paper and beans and bake it a few minutes more until it is golden and dry. I let it cool before filling it with pastry cream and fruit.
markingPoints: Weighs accurately and rubs cold fat into the flour to fine breadcrumbs
Binds without overworking, and rests the pastry in the fridge
Rolls evenly and lines the tin neatly
Blind bakes with paper and baking beans, then removes them to finish baking
Cools the case before filling it

essays.stem: Describe how to use and clean the main equipment in the pastry section safely, including the mixer, the oven and hot sugar.
essays.modelAnswer: Before using a stand mixer, I check that it is clean, that the bowl and attachment are fitted properly and that the guard is in place. I start on a low speed so that flour does not fly out. I switch it off and wait for it to stop before I scrape the bowl or change the attachment, and I never put my hand, a spoon or a spatula into a moving bowl. At the oven, I use dry oven gloves, open the door carefully to let steam out, and put hot trays on a heat-proof surface while warning others with "hot tray". When cooking sugar or caramel, I use a heavy pan, keep the handle turned in, never leave it, and add any liquid carefully because it spits. Hot sugar burns badly, so I never touch or taste it. If a burn happens, I cool it under cool running water and report it. After use, I switch off and unplug the mixer, then wash, rinse, sanitise and dry the bowl and attachments. I wipe up spills at once so that nobody slips.
markingPoints: Mixer: checks the guard and fittings, starts slowly, and switches off and waits before scraping or changing attachments
Never puts hands or tools into moving equipment
Oven: dry gloves, care with steam, hot trays on a heat-proof surface with a warning
Hot sugar: heavy pan, never left, liquids added carefully, never touched; burns cooled and reported
Switches off and unplugs, then cleans and sanitises equipment; wipes spills at once

practical1.title: Prepare, bake and plate a hot Jamaican bread pudding with crème anglaise for a villa dinner
practical1.brief: As a group, prepare, bake and plate a hot dessert for a villa dinner of 10 guests: a Jamaican bread pudding (or sweet potato pudding, if the assessor chooses) served warm with crème anglaise, from the Centre's standard recipes. One guest has a nut allergy, so check every ingredient and garnish, and keep that portion apart and labelled. Share the work: one member organises the mise en place and the tins, one makes the pudding mix, one makes the crème anglaise, and one prepares the garnish and warms the plates; a fifth member, if there is one, keeps track of the timings and the oven. Every member must also cut and plate at least two portions while the assessor watches. Bake the pudding until it is set and golden, as the recipe says. Cook the crème anglaise gently until it coats the back of a spoon, without boiling. Present 10 plates, each with a neat, equal portion, the sauce and a fresh fruit garnish, and a clean rim. Cool, cover, label and chill any leftovers quickly. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the area is clean.
materials: The Centre's standard recipes for bread pudding (or sweet potato pudding) and crème anglaise
Bread, eggs, milk, evaporated or coconut milk, sugar, butter, raisins, vanilla, nutmeg and cinnamon
Egg yolks, milk, sugar and vanilla for the crème anglaise
Fresh fruit and mint for the garnish
Scales, bowls, whisks, wooden spoons, a heavy pan, a fine sieve, baking tins and a portion guide
Oven, dry oven gloves, warm plates, labels, cling film, cleaning cloths and sanitiser
photos: Mise en place: weighed ingredients and prepared tins, with members in clean uniform
The pudding mix in the tin, before baking
The crème anglaise coating the back of a spoon
The baked pudding being cut into equal portions with a guide
Each member plating their portions (one photo per member)
The 10 finished plates, with the nut-free plate labelled
Leftovers labelled and chilled, and the area cleaned
checklist: Wore a clean uniform with hair covered, washed hands, and kept the station clean and organised
Weighed and measured ingredients accurately from the standard recipe
Carried out their own task correctly (mise en place, pudding mix, sauce or garnish)
Cooked the crème anglaise gently without boiling, or checked that it coated the spoon
Cut and plated equal portions neatly, with sauce, garnish and a clean rim
Checked ingredients for nuts, and kept the allergy plate apart and labelled
Used oven gloves and handled hot trays safely
Cooled, labelled and chilled leftovers, and cleaned and sanitised the equipment
safety: Use dry oven gloves for hot trays, and warn others with "hot tray" or "behind you"
Never boil the custard sauce; stir it over a low heat and keep pan handles turned in
Keep the allergy portion apart, made with clean equipment, and labelled
Cool leftovers quickly and chill them at 5 °C or below, or as the Centre's food safety plan says
Wipe up spills at once so that nobody slips

practical2.title: Prepare and plate a cold dessert: meringue nests with cream, tropical fruit and mango coulis
practical2.brief: As a group, prepare and plate a cold dessert for a hotel lunch of 10 guests: meringue nests filled with whipped cream and tropical fruit (such as mango, pineapple, papaya and passion fruit), with a smooth mango coulis, from the Centre's standard recipes. Share the work: one member whisks the egg whites and sugar to stiff, glossy peaks; one pipes the nests; one makes and sieves the coulis; one prepares and cuts the fruit; a fifth member, if there is one, whips the cream and chills the plates. Every member must also pipe at least two nests and plate at least two desserts while the assessor watches. Bake the nests in a low oven until they are crisp and dry, as the recipe says, and let them cool. Whip the cream just to piping consistency. Keep the cream and cut fruit chilled until plating. Put the desserts together close to service, so that the meringue stays crisp, and present 10 chilled plates with coulis, fruit and a mint leaf, and clean rims. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the area is clean.
materials: The Centre's standard recipes for meringue and mango coulis
Eggs, caster sugar, whipping or heavy cream and vanilla
Ripe mangoes and other tropical fruit, limes and mint
A clean, grease-free mixing bowl and whisk or a stand mixer, piping bags and nozzles
Baking trays lined with baking paper, a blender, a fine sieve, colour-coded boards and a fruit knife

checklist: Wore a clean uniform with hair covered, and washed hands before handling food
Used a clean, grease-free bowl and added the sugar gradually
Piped even nests of the same size
Made a smooth coulis, sieved to remove fibres and seeds
Cut fruit evenly and safely, using the right board and a sharp knife
Whipped the cream to piping consistency without over-whipping
Put together and plated the desserts neatly close to service, with clean rims
Kept the cream and fruit chilled, and cleaned and sanitised the equipment
safety: Carry knives point down, never try to catch a falling knife, and wash knives straight after use
Switch off the mixer and wait for it to stop before scraping the bowl; keep the guard in place
Keep the cream and cut fruit at 5 °C or below, or as the Centre's food safety plan says, until plating
Use dry oven gloves for hot trays, and wipe up spills at once
